description: Santa Sabina on the Aventine Hill is one of the best-preserved early Christian basilicas: a plain brick outside, rows of reused Roman columns and clear light within. Its carved wooden doors include one of the earliest surviving images of the Crucifixion.

title: An emperor’s giant head and hand sit in a museum courtyard
place: Palazzo dei Conservatori courtyard, Capitoline Museums
description: The pieces of a seated statue of Constantine, once about twelve metres tall, were found in the Basilica of Maxentius. The head, hand and feet now line the courtyard of Palazzo dei Conservatori, part of the Capitoline Museums.

title: A priest and his sons fight off sea serpents in writhing marble
description: The sculpture was dug up in a Roman vineyard in 1506, with Michelangelo among those sent to see it. Pope Julius II bought it, and it still stands in the Octagonal Court of the Vatican Museums.

title: Odysseus sails through wide painted landscapes on a Roman wall
description: These first-century BCE wall paintings were found in a house on the Esquiline Hill in 1848 and show scenes from the Odyssey in sweeping landscapes. They are now in the Vatican Museums.

title: A Roman official is buried in a coffin carved with Bible stories
description: Junius Bassus, prefect of Rome, died in 359 as a new Christian convert. His marble sarcophagus mixes Roman forms with scenes from both Testaments. It is kept in the Treasury museum of St. Peter’s Basilica.

title: A young Michelangelo signs the Virgin’s sash so no one doubts him
description: Michelangelo carved the marble in his early twenties, around 1498–99. It is the only work he ever signed. It sits behind glass in the first chapel on the right in St. Peter’s Basilica.

title: An emperor flattens a hillside to build the grandest forum of all
description: The last and largest of the imperial forums, paid for with plunder from Trajan’s wars in Dacia and finished around 112. Its column and the remains of the basilica stand beside Via dei Fori Imperiali.

title: A bronze emperor on horseback survives by being mistaken for a saint
description: The only bronze equestrian statue to survive from ancient Rome, spared because it was thought to show Constantine. The original is indoors in the Capitoline Museums; a copy stands on Michelangelo’s piazza outside.

title: Mosaics eight centuries apart share one great basilica
description: The nave mosaics date from the 430s, while the golden apse showing Mary crowned in heaven was added in the 1290s. Santa Maria Maggiore is one of Rome’s four papal basilicas, on the Esquiline Hill.

title: An obelisk carved for a pharaoh ends up beside the pope’s cathedral
place: Lateran Obelisk, Piazza San Giovanni in Laterano
description: Made for Thutmose III at Karnak, shipped to Rome for the Circus Maximus in 357, then dug up and re-erected by Pope Sixtus V in 1588. It stands in the piazza beside San Giovanni in Laterano.

title: An emperor’s daughter is buried under a dome of vine mosaics
description: This round fourth-century mausoleum was built for Constantina, daughter of Constantine, and later became a church. Its vault mosaics of grape harvests survive. It is on Via Nomentana beside Sant’Agnese fuori le Mura.

title: Christ sits among the apostles like a Roman magistrate
description: The apse mosaic of this church, from around 400, is one of the oldest in Rome, showing Christ enthroned before a city skyline. The church sits below street level on Via Urbana, near Santa Maria Maggiore.

title: A Dalmatian pope brings his homeland’s martyrs to Rome in gold
place: Chapel of San Venanzio, Lateran Baptistery
description: Pope John IV, from Dalmatia, built this chapel in the 640s for relics of martyrs from Salona and covered it in mosaics. It opens off the Lateran Baptistery beside the Archbasilica of St. John Lateran.

title: A spiral of carved soldiers climbs 30 metres into the sky
description: Finished in 113, its frieze winds 23 times around the shaft with scenes of Trajan’s wars in Dacia. The emperor’s ashes were placed in its base. It stands at the edge of Trajan’s Forum, near Piazza Venezia.

title: The Holy Family is small in a calm, ordered landscape
description: Painted around 1604 for a chapel in the Aldobrandini palace, it helped set the model for the ideal classical landscape. It now hangs in the Galleria Doria Pamphilj, a private palace gallery on Via del Corso.

title: The Jesuits build a mother church to draw in the crowds
description: The Jesuits’ main church, begun in 1568, with a wide open nave for preaching and a painted ceiling where figures seem to spill out of the frame. It stands on Piazza del Gesù, just off Via del Plebiscito.

title: A boy has been pulling a thorn from his foot for 2,000 years
description: A bronze of a boy picking a thorn from his foot, on view in Rome since the Middle Ages and much copied in the Renaissance. It is in the Capitoline Museums, in the Palazzo dei Conservatori on the Capitoline Hill.

title: Augustus wraps an altar in a peaceful procession of his family
description: An altar to peace dedicated in 9 BCE, carved with the emperor’s family in procession and scenes of plenty. It was pieced back together in the 1930s and sits in Richard Meier’s glass museum beside the Mausoleum of Augustus.

title: An emperor in armour, barefoot like a god
description: A marble statue found in 1863 at the villa of Livia, Augustus’ wife, north of Rome. Its breastplate shows the return of Roman standards from Parthia. It stands in the Braccio Nuovo of the Vatican Museums.

title: Temples, law courts and rostra crowd the valley at Rome’s heart
description: For centuries this drained valley between the Capitoline and Palatine hills was where Romans voted, traded, heard speeches and worshipped. The ruins are entered from Via dei Fori Imperiali or near the Colosseum.

title: An African-born emperor marks a victory at the Forum’s edge
place: Arch of Septimius Severus, Roman Forum
description: A triple arch from 203 celebrating Septimius Severus and his sons over the Parthians. One son’s name was later chiselled out after his brother had him killed. It stands at the northwest end of the Roman Forum.

title: Fifty thousand Romans pack an arena for games
description: Opened in 80 by Emperor Titus on the site of Nero’s palace lake, with seating for around 50,000. Later it was mined for building stone. It stands at the east end of the Roman Forum.

title: An emperor’s tomb becomes a papal fortress
description: Built as Hadrian’s mausoleum in the 130s, later turned into a fortress, prison and refuge for popes, linked to the Vatican by a raised corridor. It stands on the Tiber’s right bank, facing the Ponte Sant’Angelo.

title: Napoleon carries off an altarpiece and only half comes home
description: Perugino painted this Madonna and saints for the town council of Perugia in 1495–96. French troops took it in 1797, and its main panel never went back. It hangs in the Pinacoteca, the picture gallery of the Vatican Museums.

title: A Roman woman’s hair piled high in drilled marble curls
description: A marble bust of about 90 CE, its towering hairstyle carved with a drill, the fashion of Domitian’s court. It is in the Capitoline Museums on the Campidoglio.

title: Bernini’s colonnades open like arms in front of St Peter’s
description: Built from 1656 to 1667, the oval piazza is ringed by four rows of columns topped with saints, with an Egyptian obelisk at the centre. It is in front of St Peter’s Basilica in Vatican City.

title: A church in the Forum buried by an earthquake keeps its frescoes
description: A sixth-century church built into imperial buildings at the foot of the Palatine, sealed by a collapse in 847 and dug out in 1900. It is in the Roman Forum.

title: Roman copies of Gauls defeated by a Greek king
description: Marble copies of bronzes made for Pergamon around 220 BCE, showing Celtic warriors in defeat. The Dying Gaul is in the Capitoline Museums; the Ludovisi Gaul is in Palazzo Altemps.

title: A god’s fingers press into marble as if it were flesh
description: Bernini carved this abduction for Cardinal Scipione Borghese in 1621–22, when he was in his early twenties. It is in the Galleria Borghese, the cardinal’s villa in the Borghese gardens.

title: A man is thrown from his horse into sudden light
description: Painted in 1601 for the Cerasi Chapel, opposite Caravaggio’s Crucifixion of Saint Peter, with a horse filling most of the canvas. It is in Santa Maria del Popolo, beside Piazza del Popolo.

title: Jonah and a philosopher share a third-century coffin
description: An early Christian sarcophagus of about 270 CE that mixes biblical scenes with pagan imagery. It is kept in Santa Maria Antiqua, a buried and restored church in the Roman Forum.

title: A nymph turns into a laurel tree as a god catches her
description: Bernini carved it for Cardinal Scipione Borghese in 1622–25, with leaves and roots sprouting from her fingers and toes. It is in the Galleria Borghese, the cardinal’s villa in the Borghese gardens.

title: A striding terracotta god once stood on an Etruscan temple roof
description: A life-size painted terracotta Apollo of about 510–500 BCE from the temple at Veii, north of Rome. It is in the National Etruscan Museum at Villa Giulia, near the Borghese gardens.

title: An emperor’s arch built partly from older monuments
description: Dedicated in 315 CE after Constantine’s victory at the Milvian Bridge, it reuses reliefs taken from monuments of earlier emperors. It stands beside the Colosseum.

title: A horned Moses guards a pope’s much-shrunk tomb
description: Planned in 1505 as a huge freestanding monument, Julius II’s tomb ended up a wall tomb decades later, with Moses at its centre. It is in San Pietro in Vincoli on the Esquiline Hill.

title: A Roman Venus steps from her bath, covering herself
description: A marble copy of a Greek original related to Praxiteles’ Aphrodite of Knidos, found in Rome in the 1660s. It has its own small room in the Capitoline Museums on the Campidoglio.

title: An Etruscan couple reclines together at an eternal banquet
description: A painted terracotta coffin of about 520 BCE from Cerveteri, the man’s arm around his wife. It is in the National Etruscan Museum at Villa Giulia, near the Borghese gardens.

title: Roman soldiers carry the menorah from Jerusalem’s Temple
description: A relief inside the arch built after 81 CE to honour Titus, showing loot from the Temple after Jerusalem fell in 70 CE. The arch stands on the Via Sacra at the edge of the Roman Forum.

title: Early Christians paint the Virgin in an underground cemetery
description: Miles of tunnels used for burials from the second to fifth centuries, with what may be the oldest known painting of Mary. The entrance is on the Via Salaria, north of the centre.

title: A Roman shopping centre climbs the hillside in brick
description: Built around 100–110 CE by Apollodorus of Damascus, the curving brick complex held shops and offices over several levels. It rises above Trajan’s Forum on the slope of the Quirinal.

title: Michelangelo covers the altar wall with bodies rising and falling
description: Painted from 1536 to 1541, more than twenty years after the ceiling, with a flayed skin that may be Michelangelo’s self-portrait. It is the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican.

title: Apostles with soft, solid faces, painted before Giotto
description: Cavallini painted this fresco around 1293, and it was only uncovered in 1900 behind later choir stalls. It is in the nuns’ choir of Santa Cecilia in Trastevere.

title: Michelangelo paints Genesis on a papal chapel ceiling
description: Painted for Pope Julius II from 1508 to 1512, with nine scenes from Genesis framed by prophets and sibyls. It is the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican.

title: Three huge vaults survive from Rome’s grandest hall
description: Begun by Maxentius around 308 CE and finished by Constantine, it once held a colossal statue of the emperor. The coffered vaults of one aisle still stand on the Via Sacra in the Roman Forum.

title: A temple to all the gods under an open concrete dome
description: Built under Hadrian around 125 CE, its unreinforced concrete dome is still the world’s largest, with a nine-metre oculus. It became a church in 609 and stands on Piazza della Rotonda.

title: A stern bronze face said to be Rome’s first consul
description: A bronze head of about 300 BCE traditionally identified as Lucius Junius Brutus, founder of the Republic. It is in the Capitoline Museums on the Campidoglio.

title: Twisted bronze columns mark Saint Peter’s grave
description: Bernini’s bronze canopy, finished in 1634, stands nearly 30 metres high over the high altar and the tomb of Saint Peter. It is under Michelangelo’s dome in St Peter’s Basilica.

title: Lapis, gold and silver honour the founder of the Jesuits
place: Chapel of St Ignatius, Church of the Gesù
description: Pozzo designed this lavish altar chapel in the 1690s, where Saint Ignatius of Loyola is buried. It is in the left transept of the Gesù, the Jesuits’ mother church on Rome’s Piazza del Gesù.

title: Two heroes hunch over a board game in the middle of a war
description: A black-figure amphora signed by the Athenian potter and painter Exekias around 540–530 BCE, found in an Etruscan tomb at Vulci. It is in the Gregorian Etruscan Museum of the Vatican Museums.

title: Romans and barbarians tangle in a deep-cut marble battle
description: A 3rd-century sarcophagus with a crowded scene of Roman soldiers routing Goths, a calm general on horseback at its centre. It is in Palazzo Altemps, a branch of the National Roman Museum near Piazza Navona.

title: An athlete scrapes off oil and sweat after a contest
description: A Roman marble copy of a bronze by Lysippos, about 330 BCE, found in Trastevere in 1849. It is in the Vatican Museums, in the Pio-Clementino galleries of ancient sculpture.

title: A painted ceiling makes a church roof open to the sky
description: Pozzo’s 1691–94 nave fresco sends Saint Ignatius into heaven through painted architecture; a marble disc in the floor marks where the illusion works best. It is in the church of Sant’Ignazio near the Pantheon.

title: A sea nymph rides a shell pulled by dolphins
description: Raphael’s fresco of around 1512 for the banker Agostino Chigi’s riverside villa, with cupids aiming arrows from the sky. It is in the Villa Farnesina in Trastevere, on the west bank of the Tiber.

title: A battered bronze boxer turns his head after the fight
description: A Greek bronze from the Hellenistic period with a broken nose, cauliflower ears and inlaid copper blood. Found on the Quirinal hill in 1885, it is in Palazzo Massimo, the National Roman Museum near Termini station.

title: Bernini squeezes an oval church onto a narrow site
description: A small Jesuit church of 1658–70 that Bernini considered his best work; the oval is entered on its long side, so it feels wide rather than deep. It is on Via del Quirinale, across from the Quirinal Palace.

title: A young Jesuit lies dying in coloured marble
place: Rooms of St Stanislas Kostka, Sant’Andrea al Quirinale
description: A 1702–03 statue of the Polish novice Stanislas Kostka, with a black marble robe and white face, in the rooms where he died in 1568. It is in the novitiate beside Sant’Andrea al Quirinale.

title: Birds and fruit trees cover the walls of an underground room
description: A fresco garden from around 30–20 BCE that once lined a sunken dining room at the villa of Livia, wife of Augustus. The whole room was moved to Palazzo Massimo, the National Roman Museum near Termini station.

title: A small round temple marks where Saint Peter was said to die
place: Bramante’s Tempietto, San Pietro in Montorio
description: Bramante’s little domed shrine of around 1502 stands in a cloister courtyard and set a model for Renaissance architecture. It is at San Pietro in Montorio on the Janiculum hill above Trastevere.

title: Medusa catches sight of herself as she turns to stone
description: A marble bust of the snake-haired gorgon from the 1640s, attributed to Bernini, with a look of shock on her face. It is in the Capitoline Museums on Michelangelo’s Piazza del Campidoglio.

title: A pope’s chapel glows with gold mosaics from the 800s
description: A 9th-century church built by Pope Paschal I, known for its apse mosaics and the small gold-lined Chapel of San Zeno. It is on a side street near Santa Maria Maggiore on the Esquiline hill.

title: Over a century of architects build the world’s largest church
description: Bramante began rebuilding Saint Peter’s in 1506; Michelangelo, Maderno and Bernini followed. The basilica stands over the traditional tomb of Saint Peter in Vatican City.

title: A bronze throne floats on a burst of gilded clouds
place: Chair of St Peter, St Peter’s Basilica
description: Bernini’s 1657–66 monument encases a wooden chair said to be Saint Peter’s, held up by four Church Fathers below a window of the Holy Spirit. It fills the apse of Saint Peter’s Basilica in Vatican City.

title: A young man leans over a pool, lost in his own reflection
description: A painting from the late 1590s attributed to Caravaggio, with the youth and his reflection forming a closed circle. It hangs in the Gallerie Nazionali at Palazzo Barberini, the Baroque palace near Piazza Barberini.

title: Three workmen strain to lift an old man’s upside-down cross
description: Caravaggio painted this in 1600–01 for the Cerasi Chapel, opposite his Conversion of Saint Paul. It is still in place in Santa Maria del Popolo, the church beside the Piazza del Popolo city gate.

title: Four Roman emperors embrace on the corner of St Mark’s
description: This purple porphyry group of four co-rulers was carved around 300 AD and taken from Constantinople by Venetian crusaders in 1204. It is set into the outer corner of St Mark’s Basilica beside the Doge’s Palace gate. One missing foot was found in Istanbul.

title: A family of admirals gets painted into the Virgin’s court
place: Frari church (Santa Maria Gloriosa dei Frari)
description: Jacopo Pesaro, a bishop who led a papal fleet against the Ottomans, paid for this altarpiece and had his relatives kneel in it. Titian moved the Virgin off centre, a bold break. It still hangs on the altar it was made for, in the Frari church.

title: A Last Supper lands its painter in front of the Inquisition
description: In 1573 Veronese was questioned over the dogs, dwarfs and drunken soldiers in his Last Supper. Rather than repaint it, he changed the title. The huge canvas, painted for a Dominican refectory, now fills a wall of the Gallerie dell’Accademia museum.

title: A soldier, a nursing mother and a storm no one can explain
description: Giorgione’s small canvas of a soldier, a nursing mother and a lightning bolt has resisted every attempt at a single meaning. Two art historians look closely at it in the Gallerie dell’Accademia, the city’s main museum of Venetian painting.

title: The Coronation Mantle of Roger II of Sicily
description: Made in Norman Palermo around 1133 for Roger II of Sicily, with an Arabic inscription along its hem, the mantle was later used to crown Holy Roman Emperors. It is in the Imperial Treasury in Vienna’s Hofburg palace.

title: The Venus of Willendorf, a 30,000-year-old figure
description: This 11 cm figure, about 30,000 years old, was found in 1908 near Willendorf in the Danube valley. It is in the Natural History Museum on Vienna’s Maria-Theresien-Platz, opposite the art history museum.

title: Death and Life by Gustav Klimt
description: Klimt’s large allegory, begun in 1910 and later reworked, sets a dark figure of Death against a colourful tangle of bodies. It is in the Leopold Museum in Vienna’s MuseumsQuartier.

title: The Great Piece of Turf by Albrecht Dürer
description: Dürer’s 1503 watercolour of dandelions, grasses and plantain, studied at ground level. It belongs to the Albertina, the Habsburg palace museum in Vienna with one of the world’s great collections of drawings and prints.

title: The Hermits by Egon Schiele
description: Schiele’s 1912 double portrait shows him and his mentor Klimt as robed hermits, pressed close together. It is in the Leopold Museum, which holds the world’s largest Schiele collection in Vienna’s MuseumsQuartier.

title: The Kiss by Gustav Klimt
description: Klimt’s 1907–08 painting of an embracing couple, made with oil paint and gold leaf, and bought by the Austrian state in 1908. It hangs in the Upper Belvedere, the Baroque palace museum in Vienna.

title: The Tower of Babel by Pieter Bruegel the Elder
description: Bruegel’s 1563 painting of the biblical tower, modelled partly on the Roman Colosseum and set beside a busy Flemish harbour. It hangs in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna’s imperial picture gallery on the Ringstrasse.

title: The Crucifixion Triptych by Rogier van der Weyden
description: A small triptych from around 1440 by the Netherlandish painter Rogier van der Weyden, its three panels joined by a single landscape. It is in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna’s imperial picture gallery on the Ringstrasse.

title: Jupiter and Io by Correggio
description: Correggio’s 1530s painting of Jupiter, hidden in a dark cloud, holding the nymph Io; it was one of a series on the god’s loves. Two art historians look at it in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna’s imperial picture gallery.

title: The Three Philosophers by Giorgione
description: Giorgione’s Venetian painting from around 1509, whose three figures have been read as magi, philosophers or the ages of man. It is in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna’s imperial picture gallery on the Ringstrasse.

title: The Art of Painting by Johannes Vermeer
description: Vermeer kept this painting until his death; Hitler later bought it for his planned museum in Linz. It hangs in the Kunsthistorisches Museum on Maria-Theresien-Platz.

title: The Vienna Genesis, an illustrated sixth-century Bible
description: A sixth-century Greek manuscript of Genesis on purple vellum, with silver text and painted scenes. It is held by the Austrian National Library at the Hofburg palace.

title: Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror by Parmigianino
description: Parmigianino painted this small self-portrait around 1524 on a convex wooden panel, his hand swelling in the foreground. It is in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna’s imperial picture gallery on the Ringstrasse.

title: Portrait of Wally by Egon Schiele
description: Schiele painted his companion Wally Neuzil in 1912; seized at MoMA in 1998, it returned after a 2010 settlement with the heirs of its prewar owner. It is in the Leopold Museum in the MuseumsQuartier.

title: The Peasant Wedding by Pieter Bruegel the Elder
description: Bruegel’s 1567 wedding scene: porridge carried on a door, bagpipers and a bride beneath a paper crown. It hangs in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna’s imperial picture gallery on the Ringstrasse.

title: Seated Male Nude (Self-Portrait) by Egon Schiele
description: Egon Schiele was twenty when he painted this gaunt self-portrait in 1910, with no hands or feet. It belongs to the Leopold Museum in the MuseumsQuartier, which holds the world’s largest collection of his work.

title: The Last Judgment by Hieronymus Bosch
place: Academy of Fine Arts picture gallery, Schillerplatz
description: Hieronymus Bosch’s Last Judgment triptych fills its central panel with demons, torture machines and sinners. It hangs in the picture gallery of the Academy of Fine Arts on Schillerplatz, an art school that also famously rejected the young Hitler.

title: The Beethoven Frieze by Gustav Klimt
description: Made for a 1902 exhibition honouring Beethoven, the frieze traces humanity’s longing for happiness through monsters, nudes and a final embrace. It survives in the basement of the Secession, the white exhibition hall with a gilded laurel dome.

title: Saint Sebastian by Andrea Mantegna
description: Andrea Mantegna’s small panel sets the martyr against crumbling classical architecture and signs it in Greek. It belongs to the Kunsthistorisches Museum, the imperial picture gallery built on the Ringstrasse in the 1880s.

title: The Hunters in the Snow by Pieter Bruegel the Elder
description: Pieter Bruegel’s 1565 snowscape of weary hunters, skaters and a village below hangs in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, the Habsburg art museum on the Ring, which owns the largest group of his paintings anywhere.
